speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: BRITISH COMMONWEALTH AIR TRAINING PLAN- GENERAL POLICIES-DEMOBILIZATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as promised last week, I have a statement to make re-
garding the discussions which have taken place in connection with the British commonwealth air training.
Representatives of the Canadian and United Kingdom governments have been discussing matters of common interest to the R.C.A.F. and the R.A.F. in their overseas relations, and in connection with the British commonwealth air training plan.
The United Kingdom was represented by Captain the Right Hon. Harold H. Balfour, Under-Secretary of State for Air, and Air Marshal Sir Peter Drummond. Canada was represented by myself, Air Marshal Robert Leckie and staff officers.
Members of the R.C.A.F. are not only serving in Britain and elsewhere in Canadian squadrons, but also in their thousands axe attached temporarily to the R.A.F. squadrons, detachments, units and formations, widely dispersed throughout the world.	.
It is inevitable that innumerable questions arise concerning the welfare, careers and conditions of service of these Canadians attached to another force and for the time being serving under commanders other than Canadians. The R.C.A.F., which recruited and trained them, is responsible at all times to the people of Canada for their welfare and future prospects.
Such matters as length of service with R.A.F., commissions, promotions, operational and nonoperational tours, and leave to Canada, vitally concern not only these boys, but also their parents, dependents and friends in Canada.
From time to time adjustments must be made, and the Department of National Defence for Air, either directly or through the Canadian air officer commanding-in-chief, overseas, in conjunction with the United Kingdom air ministry, discusses and formulates the general policies which are to be followed by both forces in dealing with these important and sometimes difficult problems.
The basic agreements made between the two governments in 1939 and 1942 have been modified and amended where necessary and certain understandings have been reached which confer on us a larger measure of responsibility for our own personnel.
The policies laid down in the agreement of June 1942 have not been materially altered, but there has been clarification on some points, as well as modification of administrative procedure. The amendments to the agreements of June 1942 are tabled herewith.
Long and tough fighting lies ahead before the war is won. But we must be ready with plans for demobilization, repatriation and rehabilitation well in advance. Our problems in this

R.CA.F.-General Policies
connection are greatly accentuated because by far the largest numbers of our aircrews are serving with the R.A.F. in distant and varied theatres of war. It must be and is a matter of primary concern to the government to ensure that these men are not .placed in an unfavourable position by reason of their service in the R.A.F., or in any way handicapped as compared with men in the other Canadian services, or with their air force comrades at home. All our men must be given the same opportunities with regard to priorities in demobilization, repatriation and rehabilitation, and whilst demobilization procedure and related questions must fundamentally be the problem of each country to be dealt with in the light of the interests of its own economy and its own nationals, it is essential that our plans be closely correlated with those of the United Kingdom in order to give these benefits and advantages to our personnel when their service abroad is no longer required. To this end, it has been agreed that a joint committee of air force representatives of both countries will be established with headquarters in London, to discuss these problems, to exchange views and to advise their ministers. It has already been agreed that arrangements which have been made either by the United Kingdom or Canada for pre-demobilization, educational and vocational training shall be available to the nationals of both countries on a reciprocal basis.
Finally, a matter which, though not connected with the air training plan or its graduates but which is of considerable interest to Canadians, was also considered-that of the transfer from the R.A.F. of certain Canadian nationals who had joined that service prior to and during the early stages of the war. In this connection it has been agreed with the United Kingdom representatives that such officers and men may apply for transfer to the R.C.A.F. Certain Canadian-born women not normally domiciled in the United Kingdom who joined the Women's Auxiliary Air Force of the R.A.F. will also be eligible to apply for transfer.

My hon. friend will have to wait until the regulations with respect to transfer are issued.
Besides these personnel matters, consideration was given to the overall capacity of the training organization in Canada which is administered by Canada on behalf of the partners of the British Commonwealth air training plan. The air training plan will continue as long as the war lasts.
During the three years which followed the signing of the plan agreement in 1939, the principal. preoccupation of Canada and the other partners was to create a training organization on which could be built fighting air forces equal in size and superior in quality to those of the enemy. Today, in the beginning of 1944, it can be said that this objective has been reached, and we have increasing air superiority over the enemy in every theatre of war. This superiority is evident in the sky-fronts of the operational' theatres over land and sea. Not so evident, but behind the front line squadrons, there are thousands of aircrew being put through operational training units and conversion units, and farther back again there are tens of thousands of young aircrew going through the training schools of the British Commonwealth air training plan in Canada and in similar schools in other parts of the world.
In other words, the personnel necessary to fill squadrons, units and formations planned for the front line are already in the pipeline feeding the air forces of the United Kingdom, the commonwealth and the allies serving under the strategic direction and tactical command of the Royal Air Force. At the present time we have the capital and the necessary immediate replacements.
Our long-term war plans entail certain reductions in the numbers of entrants to aircrew training. The current entrants into training will not in fact engage the enemy for a comparatively long time. This is largely because of the increased complexity of modern aircraft requiring lengthy training over an ever widening range of subjects. The young man who fights in the air in the future will not do so until he has had more flying hours during training than ever before. In a sentence, the standards of skill required and the opportunities for obtaining experience have progressively increased since the beginning of the war.
Consequent upon the reduction in intake of trainees, there will be a gradual and progressive closing of a certain number of training units, and schools in Canada, beginning with the
Questions

R.A.F. transferred schools. The process will be deliberate and extended over many months, and the reduction of training facilities will be geared to the requisite flow of pupils through the plan.
One important objective will be to utilize to the greatest possible extent the resources in skilled personnel in our training organization as they become available, for reinforcing and enlarging the operational units. As the R.A.F. schools in Canada close, the personnel will be transferred to the operational theatre in England to increase the number of skilled men available for the continued expansion of the front line of the Royal Air Force.
Numbers of R.C.A.F. air and ground crew personnel, besides the graduates, will be made available for overseas duties owing to the reduction of training capacity in Canada and also to the curtailment of western hemisphere operations due to the more favourable war situation on our coasts.
This concentration of man-power in the United Kingdom will provide close to the front line more backing to the squadrons now actively engaged or required for forthcoming operations and renders more effective the impact of both the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. on the enemy during this critical year of the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 15, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war - Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

Yesterday at the request of the Prime Minister, I, with three other members of this house, met him and the three defence ministers, as well as the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, in a private conference. At this interview the Prime Minister read to us what we understood to be the
essential parts of the recent correspondence and other documents bearing upon the McNaughton situation.
As leader of the opposition I have certain responsibilities and obligations to this house and to the nation, and I conceive it to be my duty to make my position perfectly clear at this time. The background relevant to this picture extends over more than four years of war. Obviously a review of the more recent events could not place us in complete possession of the facts. We were told enough, however. for me to form the opinion that the Minister of National Defence in the present debate has not told the whole story. In saying that to the members of this committee and to the people of Canada I feel that I am discharging any obligations which I as leader of the opposition may have in this instance.
The responsibility now passes back to and remains with the government as to whether they will disclose the whole story fully to parliament and to the people. They and they alone are fully possessed of the background and facts. The responsibility is theirs and theirs alone. No one can share it with them. I invite the Prime Minister to make known his government's decision on this matter now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend, I am only too happy to reply to his request to make known immediately the government's position on what he has described as the "McNaughton situation" or "this matter". The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), speaking on Friday, February 11, read to the house a statement which had been issued to the press on December 27 with regard to General McNaughton. I am going to read this statement in a moment, but first I wish to say that the statement was authorized by the government, by myself and my colleagues. It was known to the government before the minister gave the statement to the press. The statement, as reported at page 411, was in the following words:
The Minister of National Defence announced to-day that following the recent illness of Lieutenant-General A. G. L. McNaughton. medical authorities have advised that he has developed a physical condition which will necessitate freedom from all military responsibility for an extended period.
General McNaughton has advised the government of his inability physically to carry on and has asked to be relieved as soon as possible.
In these circumstances and in view also of the requirements of impending operations, the minister stated that the Canadian government, with great regret, had decided to grant General McNaughton several months' leave of absence from service and to relieve him of command of the First Canadian Army. The minister paid tribute to General McNaughton's outstanding service to Canada and hoped that after a period of rest and recuperation his unusual talents
550	COMMONS
War Appropriation-General McNaughton
would be available to serve his country in some capacity less exacting than in command of an army in the field.
There is another paragraph but it is immaterial. The minister, at the time he read to the house this press release which had been issued on December 27, continuing to speak in the debate on Friday last, said:
The important points were that medical authorities had advised that the general had developed a physical condition which would necessitate freedom from all military responsibility for an extended period and that General McNaughton had advised the government of his inability physically to carry on and had asked to be relieved as soon as possible, and that the government had decided to grant General McNaughton several months leave of absence from service and to relieve him of command of the First Canadian Army.
The minister went on to say:
The advice of the medical authorities was contained in two reports which were transmitted to the Prime Minister on General McNaughton's direction and were also given to me.
There was also included General McNaughton's letter to Major-General Montague. Having these medical reports before the minister and myself and some of our colleagues, knowing that these reports would be presented to the house and made public, the government felt that it would not be advisable to go behind what was stated in the reports, to bring up other matters which might relate themselves to General McNaughton's relinquishment of command of the Canadian army. What was stated in the reports of the medical officers is perfectly clear, and it was not felt by the government, unless it was obvious that by going into other matters some useful public purpose would be served, that any statement should be made other than the one that was made up to that point.
May I say quite frankly that the Minister of National Defence himself would greatly prefer to discuss all phases of this matter to the satisfaction of every hon. member in the house. Personally, so far as he is concerned he would welcome it, and as I stated the other day he was ready at that time to give an immediate answer. My hon. friend had his immediate answer in his hand, and it was known to me what he had in mind to say. Knowing what might come to be discussed at that time, or what might arise out of the discussion, I felt it was necessary for me to say that I did not believe public policy made it advisable to say . anything further at this time with respect to what has been since referred to as the McNaughton situation. And I gave my reasons for that. May I quote them from Hansard. So that I may make the statement as comprehensive and as completely non-

evasive as possible, I shall begin with the question which was put by the hon. leader of the opposition and which appears at page 450 of Hansard of Monday, February 14:
The question is this: Were there other factors, other than ill health, which entered into the whole problem of the resignation or leave of absence of General McNaughton?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Before the leader of the opposition presses his question further, I desire to say that while I know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is prepared to answer the question immediately, as Prime Minister I have very grave doubts whether it is not against public policy to discuss further at this time the matter which is raised by the question which the hon. gentleman has asked.
I gave my reasons for that, and they were set out in the course of the discussion. I shall quote one paragraph which appears on page 453 of Hansard. I said:
The government's action in this matter, as I have already said, is entirely begotten of a desire to protect the war effort not only of this country but of the united nations to the fullest extent possible and to protect all parties concerned therewith.
I felt it was owing to this house and to the country that so far as the correspondence was concerned the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other two parties whom I invited should come and see the correspondence and read it with me. I also invited a former minister of national defence in a previous administration, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) to accompany them. I placed the correspondence, or rather read, as the leader of the opposition has just said, the essential parts of the correspondence to them. I have left it to these hon-. gentlemen to act in this matter as their own consciences may dictate. I have placed no restriction upon them with respect to the information they gained at that interview, which lasted for three hours, and in which all that is really essential in what has been described as the McNaughton situation was gone into very fully.
I want to repeat at this moment what I said the other day in replying to the leader of the opposition:
Before the leader of the opposition presses his question further, I desire to say that while I know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is prepared to answer the question immediately, as Prime Minister I have very grave doubts whether it is not against public policy to discuss further at this time the matter which is raised by the question which the hon. gentleman has asked.
Hon. members of this house know that at the present time preparations are being made on a vast scale for the invasion of Europe. The question that I 'have to ask myself is

War Appropriation-General McNaughton
this: Is any further discussion of what has been referred to as the McNaughton situation likely to have a good or an adverse effect on the war effort of Canada, of Great Britain, of the United States and of other of the united nations. I believe that the morale, not only of the people in the countries I have mentioned but more particularly of the armies not of Canada alone but of the other countries might be very seriously affected were there to be at this time a discussion which went into a number of matters that have taken place in the past. Such a discussion might provoke a very serious condition of affairs if begun at this time.
I want to make it perfectly clear the government has nothing to hide or conceal in this matter. The minister wishes to conceal nothing. Indeed he would prefer, for his own feelings and for personal reasons, to have without reservation matters disclosed which were disclosed to the leaders yesterday; but as Prime Minister I have a great responsibility to safeguard the war effort of all the united nations; and I repeat, I doubt very, very much if it would not be against public policy to discuss the matter further at this time. So far as the government is concerned I intend not to discuss it or have it discussed unless some hon. gentlemen opposite or others outside should, by statements that may be made, render it necessary for the government to make disclosures which up to the present time have not been made.

As one of those present at yesterday morning's meeting I should like to say that I came away with the impression that it would not be in the public interest at this time to discuss this matter more fully than it has been discussed. I must say. this, however, that the discussion this afternoon by the leader of the opposition and the Prime Minister is bound to arouse in the public mind a good many questions. If those questions arise it seems to me there are two things to be considered. First there is the matter of the public interest, and in that I am in agreement with the Prime Minister. Then there is the viewpoint of the other party concerned, namely Lieutenant General McNaughton himself, a man who has served this country well, whose great talents in organizing the Canadian army I think are recognized by everyone in the house. In view of the fact that General McNaughton has submitted a letter in which he gave as the reason for his request the fact that his health was poor, as apparently it was, it seems to me that we should take into consideration General McNauehton's great service to this country;
and if we wish to pursue this matter further, in my opinion a committee of the house should meet General McNaughton and discuss matters with him.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say just one word. I do not know of anyone who is more sensitive, and perhaps wrongly so, to any suggestion of lack of frankness or candour than I am. I have spoken to this committee twice concerning this matter, and in the statements I made I think I endeavoured to state clearly that I was not saying everything there was to be said in connection with this regrettable episode but that I was dealing with the particular matter which counted, namely the question of the granting of leave of absence to General McNaughton and the reasons for it.
It does cut just a little for my hon. friend to proclaim this afternoon, in one short sentence, that he has come to the conclusion that the Minister of National Defence has not told the whole story. I can see that in headlines across Canada. The Minister of National Defence has made it clear to this committee that he has not told the whole story of the McNaughton situation.
The question is whether or not the Minister of National Defence has anything to hide. That is the important thing. My hon. friend has not suggested that there is anything of that kind, and he has had the opportunity to become acquainted with the communications in connection with this matter. Perhaps my hon. friend did not mean anything by it, but to have that statement made as it was does not help, when at page 413 of Hansard of February 11 I said we could go into all these matters, mentioning the rumours, the press reports, the off the record statements, and so on, and then said:
We could go into all of this as well as any other matters relating to the subject. I would prefer not to do so because such discussions can. to say the least, do no possible good, especially at times like these.
Again at page 449 of Hansard I said I did not think the morale of the Canadian people or the morale of the troops in the field would be promoted by the discussion of factors which at the moment and in the circumstances can have no application. A little later I repeated that I would prefer not to discuss any other factors. I only want to say to the committee that if my hon. friend has any suggestion to make that the portion of the story I have not told, and which I indicated I had not told, contains anything which he thinks I desire to hide, I want him to say so now. I would have preferred, as the Prime Minister has said, to go into this matter from
552	COMMONS
War Appropriation-General McNaughton
stem to gudgeon, for the simple reason that it would have prevented any possible suspicion or suggestion that I or the government had anything to hide. I assented to the course which the Prime Minister has indicated this afternoon for the reasons he gave, namely in the public interest, which was concurred in by the leader of the C.C.F. party. The leader of the opposition has made no expression on that point.
I am gratified by the fact that although there has not been a disclosure to the house of the whole situation, the government has indicated that it has no desire whatever to keep the communications within the confines of governmental privacy but has made them available to three hon. members of this house, with no strings of any kind attached except the dictates of their own conscience. Under those circumstances I do submit that it was hardly fair-I do not generally criticize him for this, and I repeat that he may not have intended it in this way-for my hon. friend to say that he had come to the conclusion, as if it were something he had only discovered after seeing these communications, that the Minister of National Defence had not told the whole story. I have said I have not told the whole story; I said that to the committee on two occasions. The purpose of the conference with these hon. gentlemen was to let them know the whole story. I do ask my hon. friend, if he thinks there is anything I have to hide in connection with this matter, to indicate that fact; or if he did not intend the reflection which I feel he cast upon my statement, I ask him to say so.

I had no idea that the
minister was reading into my remarks something which I think upon reflection he will see is not there.
Oh, 'oh.

May I say to hon.
gentlemen to my right that I heard several remarks from that corner imputing motives of one kind or another to the leader of the opposition. I think most hon. members of this house know of my desire to be fair to the government and everyone else. No one understands that better than the minister, I am sure; otherwise perhaps I should be in some state of heated anger over this matter. Instead of that I am trying to discuss it reasonably, and I hope the minister and the committee will understand that. If the minister will accept my statement in the reasonable way in which it was made, I simply said -that we were told enough for me to
fMr. Ralston.]
come to. the conclusion that in the present debate the Minister of National Defence has not told the whole story. It may be that the minister and I are looking at these words and their context in entirely different ways, but I want to tell the minister that what I wanted to convey, and what I think is conveyed as clearly as that could be done, is that after having gone over certain of the correspondence and other documents which were shown to us I came to the conclusion that the whole story had not been told.
That was already clear.

I quite understand that, but I do not understand why the minister makes an issue of this. Both my hon. friend and the Prime Minister made the point clear, when the debate was halted last Monday evening, that there were some facts which the government felt should not be disclosed to the house and the country because of the public interest. All right. Surely it is not wrong for me, after having seen the documents, to come to a conclusion, as I did; and if that conclusion was the same as that reached by the minister, so much the better.

There is just one point
between us; that is, that my hon. friend's statement suggested that he had to see the documents before coming to the conclusion that the minister had not told the whole story. My point is that the minister himself indicated to the committee on at least two occasions that he was not disclosing all the circumstances, and that it did not require the conference, which is the suggestion contained in my hon. friend's statement, in order to give him the information from which he could conclude that the minister had not disclosed everything.

My statement was simfdy an attempt to tell the committee what were my conclusions after having the correspondence read to me. The minister had told us that the full story was not being disclosed, but after all it seemed necessary, the evidence having been presented to me, to form my own conclusions, and that is exactly what I did. I do not want the minister to take umbrage. Perhaps he is a little bit touchy, and perhaps I would be if I were in his position. I do not want him to go away with the idea, and I do not want any one in the house to think that I had some ulterior motive in formulating that sentence. I tried to make it just as fair as I could.
