speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the committee wants to see this matter thoroughly discussed, although it may not be properly before the committee. Therefore it would be in order for hon. members to rise now and1 speak on what we are discussing at the present time before taking another subject.

A moment ago the Prime Minister referred to the discussion which took place last Monday in connection with the resignation of or leave of absence granted to General McNaughton. That discussion had taken place because of the following question put to the Minister of National Defence by the leader of the opposition:
My question is whether or not any factors, other than that which he mentioned of ill-health, entered into the resignation of General McNaughton.
The Prime Minister intervened in the debate in order to put an end to the discussion, and he said:
I should be pleased to meet with and to show the correspondence to the leader of the opposition and to the leaders of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit parties.
He also added the hon. member for Yale to that group. The Prime Minister completely ignored another group in this house, the Bloc Populaire of Canada. He knows of the existence of this group at least since the by-elections at Stanstead and Cartier. If any group in this house is entitled to information, then all groups should be entitled to the same information. If any member is entitled to any information, then all members should be entitled to the same information. What right has one group to get information which another group cannot get? What right has the hon. member for Yale to get information which other hon. members of this house cannot get? Have we any rights in this parliament? Is this a democratic parliament? Are we not entitled as members of parliament to all information?
If there is some secret about the matter, then close the doors like we have done in the past. I do not want any secrets to be revealed to the enemy, but I think it is unfair when the Prime Minister takes it upon himself to call in the leaders of certain groups and another member who is not a leader of any group in order lo give out information and ignore the others. That is my view, and because that is my view I put this question to the Minister of National Defence. Were there other factors other than ill health which entered into the whole problem of the resignation or leave of absence of General McNaughton?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not sorry my hon. friend' has raised the point as to why hon. gentlemen besides those whom I named the other day were not included in a meeting to discuss a confidential matter with myself as the leader of the government. That brings me back to procedure under the British parliamentary system. That system recognizes the government, recognizes it as the body which has been entrusted by the people to carry on the business of the country, and it recognizes the opposition. The position of the opposition has been recognized by our House of Commons in the enactment, of a statute which gives an official position to the leader of the opposition. The government and the opposition are the two elements of parliament which under the British system are presumed to be the ones to be considered, in the main may I put it, in carrying on the business of the country.
At the time I extended the invitation I did, I asked myself whether I should not confine to the leader of the opposition the invitation I was extending to discuss privately a matter of great public importance. I would have been taking a proper position if I had so confined my invitation. The leader of the opposition himself took exception to the fact that I had not conferred with him earlier. He recognized that he had certain rights as the leader of the opposition to know some matters which were of great public importance but which necessarily had to be kept secret. I gave him the reason why I had not asked him earlier to confer with me. I knew very well that if he had been given certain information in a private way before there was any discussion in parliament he might have felt himself precluded from debating as freely as he otherwise might have wished to do and from giving information to the members of his party.
The reason I extended an invitation to the leaders of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit party is that throughout this entire parliament there has been a recognition that at the time of the last general election those parties were returned in the numbers in which they were. Their leaders in this house have been granted, not as a matter of right but as a matter of courtesy, a certain recognition by the government. It seemed to me that the present was an occasion where it was desirable to invite those hon. gentlemen to a conference. The reason for inviting the hon. member for Yale must be obvious to all members of the house. The hon. member for Yale is a member of the privy council of Canada and has served in the position of minister of national defence under a Conservative administration. I felt that it

554	COMMON'S
War Appropriation-General McNaughton
would help to give confidence to hon. members of the house and to the public if the hon. member for Yale were present at that interview.
But for my hon. friend to say that because a new party has come into existence since a [DOT] by-election, the leader of that party should have the same courtesy extended to him, is I think to take a position that is perfectly ridiculous. If that procedure is to be followed we may expect that any number of hon. gentlemen may suddenly become leaders of parties, whether small in number or not, and claim special rights and privileges in this house. I would have felt that I was making a Very great departure from the proper procedure in parliament if I had gone any further in recognizing groups as a part of the opposition than I did.
May I say that I intend as far as it lies within my power to see that the business of this House of Commons is discussed as between the government and the opposition. If the opposition wish to be divided into groups, that of course is their own affair. I would draw attention to this fact. They are rapidly heading toward the system which developed in France where there was a large number of parties and where the business of the country got into such a state that there was no stability. I think quite sincerely that that condition had a good deal to do with the fate of the world as it is to-day. I do not believe the people of Canada wish to see a lot of parties in this country and I as Prime Minister am not going to do anything to further that trend.

Before proceeding to say what I had intended to say, I should like to say just one word to the Prime Minister with respect to the formation of parties. The fundamental reason why new parties form is that the men in power signally fail, and the people, feeling absolute frustration because of their inability to get what they want from those in power, form new parties. I tell the Prime Minister that just as long as he fails to give the people of Canada what they want in the way of distribution of goods so that they can enjoy a standard of living commensurate with what their productive power justifies, he must expect to see new parties form ad infinitum in this country, and the one who will be to blame will be the Prime Minister himself. He. cannot escape responsibility by rising and giving eloquent discourses and reading lectures to us every once in a while.
The Prime Minister speaks as though Canada were the only country in which more

than two parties were recognized in parliament. If I am correctly informed, in England at the present time the Liberal party forms the third party and receives recognition. Also, if I am correctly informed, for a time in the mother of parliaments the Irish party formed the third party and was freely granted recognition. Consequently the Prime Minister is not breaking altogether new ground, although we recognize that he has endeavoured to be fair and just in his treatment of the minorities in parliament since he has been leading the government.
With respect to the McNaughton case, I had the impression before it was ever discussed in parliament that it was one which it would be altogether in the public interest for us to leave pretty much alone, leaving it to the government in power which is in a position to know all the details; and my experience yesterday in the meeting to which the Prime Minister referred confirmed me in that belief. I would say now that if we would discharge our responsibility as members of this house we would discontinue the discussion of this McNaughton affair and allow it to work its own way out in time.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say. As a private member I cannot understand the distinction that is made with respect to matters which can be told to the leader of the opposition and the leaders of certain groups in this house but which cannot be told to private members. The Prime Minister was right when he said .that in England there is only one leader of the opposition officially recognized by the government. Then he added that he had extended the courtesy to the leaders of two ' other groups, the C.C.F. group and the New Democracy group, of calling them into his confidence. But if the practice in England is to be followed, the government shall consider only the leader of the official opposition; but if similar courtesies are extended to the leaders of two other groups, that same courtesy should be extended to all members.
I do not see why the leaders of the C.C.F. and New Democracy groups should receive better treatment than my hon. friend the member for Laval-Two Mountains, the leader of the Canadian party, or the leader of the Bloc Populaire, or the member for North Battleford, or the new member for Cartier. They should all be extended the same courtesy as is already extended to two leaders of political groups.
What are the matters that can be told only to the leaders and not to the rank and file? How is it that the rank and file cannot get

War Appropriation-General McNaughton
certain information and that they are not trusted? Last year or the year before I suggested that we should have secret sittings of the house regularly once a week, when the government should take the members "into their confidence and tell them matters that would not be discussed in public. There is news appearing in the press which has a much more disturbing effect on the morale of the Canadian people than the McNaughton case, especially the bombing of those seventeen allied ships at Bari in Italy by German aeroplanes, with no counter-attack from the allies. Those ships were not protected. That story appeared in the press, in every paper. Is not a thing of that kind disturbing to the morale of the Canadian people? Does it not give them the impression that there is something wrong? Those shiploads of ammunition and supplies were for the 8th Army and the 5th Army. Who was punished for allowing the ships to be sunk? Nobody was. Eisenhower was sent to England, and Montgomery had his picture taken with the Minister of National Defence. Nobody was punished. Seventeen allied ships loaded with ammunition bombed at an Italian port by the Germans without retaliation, it must have a disturbing effect on the morale of the Canadian people and of all the allied nations.
When there is something wrong in the Department of National Defence it is often said that the facts cannot be told because it is a military secret. Last year when I fought for the health of those in the Canadian army and wanted to see that the boys who were unfit were discharged because they were a burden to the army as well as to the taxpayers of this country, I was jeered by some members who said they were bored in listening to the dialogue carried on about it. between the Minister of National Defence and myself. Here I must mention that one of our colleagues who deserves special praise is the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Halifax, who has seen that many grievances were redressed.
Another case that is very sad is that of a boy who was unfit for the army. He suffered from angina pectoris. He was first classified "C-2" by his doctor. Then he went to the army and was classified "B." He was called up again and was classified "A." He drilled for a day, fell sick and called for a doctor. That was refused. They found the boy dead the morning after and later on he was buried in my constituency, where he was born. When a man dies under such circumstances the case deserves consideration, and deserves what else? It deserves reform. It is time for reform. We are here to talk about public business, and this is public business.
100-36J
There is also a man in the camp at Barriefield who has to follow a special diet of veal liver and things like that, a regimen recommended by a specialist who knows his case, and he has to go to the restaurant to buy this special food out of his meagre pay. He has fallen off in weight from 142 to 108 pounds, and he is very sick. But he is kept there. He cannot follow the regimen prescribed in camp, but he is kept there just the same. There are many cases like that, and I feel that it is time to consider the health of the men in the army. We should see that the boys in every branch of the army are kept in good health. These are matters that should be discussed.
Why did not the leader of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F., the leader of the New Democracy group, the leader of the Bloc Populaire and the leaders of all other groups ask the government to explain what happened at Bari and who was responsible there? Was it Montgomery? Was it Eisenhower? Who was responsible for not protecting those seventeen ships loaded with ammunition and food for the 8th Army along the Adriatic coast? Perhaps the reason why the allied advance is so slow in Italy is that those boys did not have the ammunition. It is time to ask the government about it. Is it not much more important than McNaughton's resignation?

(Translation) Mr. Speaker, the first part of the resolution at present under consideration reads as follows:
1. That sums not exceeding $3,650,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1945, for
(a) the security, defence, peace, ordqr and welfare of Canada;
I shall confine my remarks mainly to paragraph (a) of the resolution at present under consideration: "the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada". Here are words which are frequently misused. The government is asking this house to vote $3,650,000,000 to ensure the realization of security, defence, peace, order and welfare, but is it taking the necessary action to achieve this purpose? We shall see. Strikes are breaking out everywhere. Dissatisfaction is rife. Unemployment is increasing, and trouble makers are taking advantage of this deplorable situation which borders upon disorder. Since the mobilization of all our resources for the prosecution of an exaggerated war effort, similar appropriations have been requested each year from parliament for a similar purpose. But, are we not standing still? Nay, we are going backwards. Never has the national debt reached such a high level. Never have taxes weighed so heavily
War Appropriation-Army

upon the taxpayer. The public must put up with restrictions of all kinds. The Canadian family is dealt a heavy blow by the absence of the mother working in war plants. Add to this the insidious propaganda broadcast over the radio in such terms as these: "The woman of the day is the woman in uniform." In spite of the feeling of admiration I have for our women soldiers, I believe, as many others do, that the woman of the day is still the mother, who is especially revered because of the lives she has given and still gives to the nation. Notwithstanding all the sacrifices and the nobleness of the woman in uniform, I prefer to see the woman in her splendid role of guardian of the home, or preparing herself to fulfil such an admirable task.
Where did the popularity of feminine enlistments originate? If I am not mistaken, it started in totalitarian countries, in Soviet Russia, especially. Although such a statement may seem paradoxical, I am not a supporter of order within disorder nor of disorder within order. And what is the worst disorder, if not the breaking up of the family, which is the very foundation of society? I will not support this measure, not only for the reasons I have just indicated, but also because a revolution is in process of preparation in Canada. The government seems to do nothing to prevent its blazing out sooner or later, even before the end of this conflict. Is any evidence required? Only yesterday a party which has assumed a new name held a congress. That party has always been considered as banned in this country.
They changed their name.

I agree with my hon. friend from Portneuf. Because that party has assumed a new name while holding the same doctrine, the government adopts toward it a laisser faire policy. Only a few days ago, prominent members of the clergy gave to the authorities of the city of Montreal a solemn warning about playgrounds where communistic propaganda is at work among our young people. They have furnished so much evidence in support of their claims that aldermen of the city of Montreal have asked for an inquiry into the matter. The pursuit of a policy of iaisser-faire has brought us to such a pass. Moreover, after this frightful war, which is engulfing the economy of the nation has come to an end, who will be the cat's-paw? Who will hold sway over all of central Europe? And what will Canada have to offer her sons and daughters whose careers, shattered or in such a state that they must be built up again from scratch, will be to them an

even heavier burden that the wounds they suffered on the battle-fields? Let us first look after our own. Our freedom and our rights as Canadian citizens come first. Away with agitators, with propaganda agents of subversive ideas.
Since the government asks for this sum of
13,650,000,000 to ensure the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada, it is my right and duty to ask that it safeguard without delay our threatened peace, security and social order. Since the government intends to bleed white the Canadian taxpayer in order to defend Christianity, freedom, justice and right, I would ask, in the name of every sacred principle, that it put a stop before it is too late to the insults and mud hurled every day at Christianity and His Holiness the Pope by the advocates of communism and by the sheet called "The Gospel Witness". On page fifteen of its issue dated February 10, this paper ran the following monstrosity:
(Text)
More About Russia and the Vatican
Last week we quoted an article from Izvestia, Soviet newspaper, which asserted that "servility of the Vatican towards fascism has not been confined to Italy," etc.	Izvestia's article is
criticized by the New York Times as being "unjust and intemperate." The press dispatch was as follows:
"New York, Feb. 4.-The attack on the Vatican by the Soviet government newspaper Izvestia is denounced to-day by the New York Times as 'unjust and intemperate.'
" 'Of all the incendiary literary bombs manufactured in Moscow since the Teheran conference and thrown with such light-hearted recklessness into the unity of the allied nations, none is likely to do greater damage,' the Times says. It adds that the 'palpable insincerity' of Izvestia's charges may be judged by the character of one of them.
"The Times asserts that Russia's allies, Britain and the United States, 'have no doubt where the real sympathy of the Vatican lies in this struggle.'
" 'They recognize the inescapable neutrality of the Pope's position,' it says, 'but they have had no difficulty in finding in his eloquent declarations clear evidence of his detestation for those who have violated the rights of little nations, who have committed bestial acts from one end of Europe to the other and who have attempted to elevate the dogma of totalitarianism to the dignity of a new religion.'
"The Times' defence of the Roman Catholic church should not be taken seriously, as it has long been evident that on many matters it takes its orders from the Roman hierarchy in the United States. Like other daily papers, it probably has one or more Romanist editorial writers, and one of them in all probability is responsible for this. Nothing escapes the eye of the propaganda department of the Roman Catholic church. It makes use of the radio and the public press for the dissemination of its views. The Roman serpent is a hydra-headed monster; and every head has a thousand tongues speaking lies and blasphemy.

War Appropriation-Army
(Translation) Neither communism nor this nameless sheet take into account the fact that millions of Roman Catholics and Christians of various denominations fight in the ranks of the united nations. Unless the government stop this propaganda at its very origin, Canada is in for a dismal future. These people will avail themselves of the deep post-war reactions to overwhelm established authorities both religious and civil. Demobilization in the army and the industries will .afford them a fertile field for the dissemination of the most subversive doctrines. On the heels of destitution and unemployment the conflagration will spread to every part of the country. That is why I urge the government to take every necessary step to safeguard security, peace and order in Canada.
After the filthy extract written by a coward, I wish to read a touching description from the pen of a soldier-priest who, among thousands, has fallen a victim to German bullets on the blessed soil of Belgium. This extract is taken from Nouvelles catholiques, issued by the Wartime Information Board, on February 1, 1944:
While Awaiting the Firing Squad
While awaiting to be shot by a German firing squad, Father Joseph Peters, rector of Comblain-au-Pont, Liege diocese, wrote the following letter to his parishioners-a last message from "Your pastor who loves you and will continue to do so in heaven."
Father Peters recalls that every day he has offered the following prayer to Almighty God: "From this day, I accept with all my heart and with perfect joy, any kind of death that it might please Thee to choose for me, with all its difficulties, anguish and sufferings." The letter adds: "The time has come to realize this promise. When you receive this letter, I shall have fallen a victim to German bullets for having served my country as a priest and a soldier.
"I have no time to relate to you how and why I have acted but I shall say that I have no regret for what I have done and would do it again if I could.
"I face death without fear or blame, relying on Almighty God's infinite mercifulness and convinced that He will welcome me to heaven, where I hope to meet my dear parents, my brothers and sisters who have preceded me in the eternal world to come.
"Is it not true that you must know how much I loved you without distinction of age, rank or party, and I have felt, especially from the time of my incarceration, that you loved me as a father. . . .
"Before being called to face my supreme judge, I wish to beg forgiveness from anyone whom I may have offended in any way or toward whom I may have neglected to do any good deed which it was in my power to do. . . .
"My dear brethren, I must leave you in the act of blessing you for the last time . . . and,
for the last time, I shout: 'All for Almighty God and the Blessed Virgin Mary! Long live the Catholic Church! Long live Belgium! Long live Comblain-au-Pont'."
(The Universe, December 17.)
How many times have I urged the government to ban the newspaper The Gospel Witness, sower of hatred and national disunity. This accursed sheet spreads falsehood, calumny and abuse even against the united nations and slings mud at their noblest characters. And the Post Office department welcomes its antinational undertakings by accepting its infamous propaganda for distribution all through the country. That is the pass to which things have come. We are fighting for the triumph of Christianity, freedom, justice and human rights, while in Canada there are two kinds of justice, one for the reviler of Christianity and the heroes of this war, and the other for the man who for a period of nearly four years has languished in an internment camp and was denied a trial. If it is for such a justice that we are sacrificing all our resources and that we are asked to vote again $3,650,000,000, I say that it is indeed not worth while. Therefore, we call upon the government to stop persecuting that outstanding citizen who has been and still is, whatever anyone may think, the former mayor of Montreal -and member for St. Mary in the Quebec legislature.
I shall make one further remark before I conclude. The statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) gives little encouragement, as regards our reserve army and the men who have been mobilized. I am very much afraid that conscription for service anywhere and on any war theatre, although now an accomplished fact, will be enforced even more sternly. No one has opposed more than I such a policy: Therefore, I bring once again to the attention of the government the difficulties they will face in the dangerous course they have long since taken. I repeat that I have never approved of that policy, that I condemn it more than ever as forcibly as I can.

I am not a leader of a
group like the last1 speaker, therefore I have no speech to read; but I wish to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the government, certain facts about the question which, fortunately or unfortunately, has been raised in this house this afternoon. After all is said and done, we are in the fifth year of the war. I think this country has done splendidly on the land and1 sea and in the air, starting as it did from scratch. I wish to say to the noble seven who sit down in the left-hand corner
War Appropriation-Army

that their province was one of the most exposed of all. In all our eastern provinces as well we were very fortunate that we did not have an invasion with the gestapo, the trampling feet, the loud speaker, the whip, the concentration camps and the deportation of large numbers of the civiliain population to Germany and other places. We were spared all these cruelties and dangers which might have happened to this country.
I believe it is the opinion of .the private members and of people outside the house that the country has responded nobly in this emergency. I am not here to criticize anybody, but I wish to say that the public are paying for the war, and they are entitled to know the facts. I am speaking only as a private member. I do not know anything about it. I was not told anything, and I do not want to be told anything, because I have already heard a great deal of the story from those who have come home from the front. I repeat that when the war broke out the government were confronted, as in the last war, with an emergency 'because we had thrown away our land, sea and air forces and qur friends as well. We had simply disbanded our army, navy and air foroe. The permanent force was laughed at. Look at the men who are leading the armies on the front to-day. Many of them, were then in the permanent force. I remember many of them. When they walked down the streets of the cities they were looked upon by pacifists with derision .and it was said that they should be out of the profession altogether. These men saved us and have done nobly.
I desire to say a word about what was done by the British government in a case like this. As you all know, away back in January last year the war was not going very well in Africa. Mr. Churchill, the Prime Minister, went over to Africa. General Wavell, General Auchin-lech and General Ritchie were transferred, and the march across the desert was placed in charge of General Alexander and General Montgomery. They marched right across the desert, and after Casablanca they met the army coming from America. In the British House of Commons private members rose- some of them just back from the front-and criticized. At the time I gave a copy of the British Hansard to the Minister of National Defence (Army) and it showed that private members in the British House of Commons, many of them generals, many of them from the army, the navy and other places, 'had criticized the conduct of the war. Mistakes will always 'be made in war; but the mistakes which the British have made are as nothing compared with the mistakes which Germany

made and the mistake she made by forcing Japan to attack Pearl Harbor, forcing the United States into the war.
It is all very well for our friends down in the left-hand corner to talk about small nations. We have seen what happened to small nations in Europe. We would have had the same thing happen here if it were not for the mother country and the stand taken by the people of Canada and the government in raising such a noble army, navy and air force. The people want to know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about this matter. It was discussed1 after Africa in the British House of Commons and Mr. Churchill told the house the truth. I should like to point out also what they did in Germany and in Russia regarding a similar situation. At Stalingrad the Germans and t'he Russians brought in numbers of new generals. They removed a great many generals. Both the Russians and the Germans brought in managers of departmental stores and others who were civilians. They had learned to drill in two years or less. The new generals did a magnificent job. The Russians under new generals started their march at Stalingrad and they have defeated the Germans all along the line. I point these things out to the committee because it is not an involved question at all. I pointed out yesterday that the commitments which are being made are so vast and the world war is so widespread that it is hard for the average citizen, unless he follows the thing and has been following military matters many years, to know very much about it.
We are a nation and there is no intention on the part of the British government to interfere with our status, our sovereignty or our autonomy. We entered this war voluntarily by a resolution of the house which, with one or two exceptions, had the full support of the members. That resolution told the government to give the full strength and the full power of the nation to the conduct of the war. It was well that Canada decided to do so because she had to start from scratch, and as I say, our forces have done splendid work on the land and sea and in the air.
It do not believe it is the duty of the opposition, as their leader has said, to decide this matter of policy. The onus is on the government of the day as long as they are the government of the day to conduct a total war in a manner that will satisfy the people who are paying the taxes. This war was forced upon the British empire. Nobody wanted it. The empire went to the limit to have peace. It disarmed, threw away all its defences in 1922, 1923 and 1924. It had nothing left when

War Appropriation-Army
the war broke out. In the period of twenty years between the two wars, the most fatal in the history of civilization, we thought we could do without armies, navies and air forces and depend on notes and the result was the British empire was left by the pacifists in a helpless condition. If the people are not allowed to know the facts, if they are allowed to know just what their rulers decide, then we are embarking on a very dangerous course.
Yesterday I referred to what Mr. Eden said in the British House of Commons on December 7, and on December 14, Mr. Churchill having taken sick, he referred to the commitments which had been made at Cairo between Great Britain, United States and China. These nations were represented by Mr. Churchill, Mr. Roosevelt and Chiang Kai-shek. They came to certain conclusions which bound Canada. These conclusions were that in the Pacific so far as the war against Japan was concerned everything that Japan gained at Pearl Harbor in December 1941 would be taken from her; that Japan would also have to give back everything she had acquired in the Pacific in the last two generations. Nobody knows when the war with Germany is going to end. I believe the full facts should be given this afternoon to the people of Canada. We should know the ins and outs of this case. I read in the house last year a statement of Major Markland, V.C., who is serving in this war. He is a member of the British House of Commons. There are forty-six members of the British House of Commons who have lost their lives in this war and all but one or two are Conservatives. Major Markland, Y.C., rose and criticized the conduct of the war in North Africa, whereupon Mr. Churchill gave a full statement to the house, and to the public later on the radio, with regard to the transfer of generals and all that kind of thing. The conduct of the war for Canada is the responsibility of the government and the officers on the field and no one else. I do not want to say anything to interfere with the progress of the war or in any way to impede the work of the government or the minister in that connection; because I think the opposition as a whole has so far given the government splendid support. To ask us to throw out the life-line as to what should be done on government policy now is another matter, when we have nothing to do with it. I am not speaking for any party in this house. I have been nothing but a consistent follower of one party all my life. I have never claimed to be anything else. I have been a supporter of rearmament all along the line, in season and out of
season. I was a voice crying in the wilderness in the period between the two wars, when I said we should not leave the defence of civilization to notes, pacifist doctrines, the Monroe doctrine, and all that kind of thing. I supported, to the best of my ability, the expenditure of money on our defences, and in 1935, when I was sitting on the other side of the house, I opposed the reduction in the defence estimates that was made by my own . government before the election of that year.
I regret the stand that the government has taken regarding a great "soldier, statesman and patriot" whom I have known since he was a student at McGill university. I do not know anything about the conduct of the war in Italy except what I have heard, though I believe there is one matter which might well be mentioned here. In this world war there has been too much dependence upon those who have graduated from staff colleges. I understand some of the best men in the field in this war are men who have been connected with the militia all their lives, men who have gone up the ladder from the bottom to the top, and in connection with our army, navy and air force I think it might have been better if that principle had been followed in this war a little more liberally than has been the case so far.
That is about all I have to say. I believe this is a matter for the government to decide, and I am sorry it has gone as far as it has because I believe the people are entitled to know the truth. Mistakes will always be made during a war. Mistakes have been made in connection with the Germans all down through history, and mistakes will be made in the future. Many more mistakes will be made before the end of this war unless this House of Commons reasserts itself. Talk about parliamentary control over the war! The private members of this house might just as well pack up and go home if we are just to take somebody's say-so in connection with the conduct of the war. I am strongly opposed to the stand taken by the Prime Minister and the government in this matter. I believe the people are entitled to all the facts. All the cards should be laid on the table; if that is done we will strengthen the morale of the people of Canada and of the troops at the front, who cannot say anything because they have lost their civilian status. They can say nothing at all; their civilian rights have been taken away, and it is up to us to protect our men in the field and the people at home. After all, wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen at the front, and not by home defence. I suggest to the noble seven down at the far end of the chamber that there is no such thing
War Appropriation-Army

as home defence, as the small nations of Europe found out to their sorrow. The mechanized hordes rolled right over the small nations. Canada has to stand with the mother country in this fight; we have to hang together or we shall hang separately, because none of the dominions is able to go it alone.

I should like to ask the minister a question on the first item in his estimates, if am in order now. If my question is not in order I shall not expect the minister to answer it now. Yesterday in Toronto I found a good deal of excitement being caused by the calling up for service of eighteen year old lads going to high schools and collegiates. A man whom I know very well, who has one son nineteen years of age now in the air force and another lad nearly seventeen, called me up in reference to his neighbour's son. This boy is just past eighteen, and a day or two ago he received a call to report to military headquarters. My question is this. Has it come to that stage, that lads in Toronto and perhaps elsewhere, eighteen years of age, are being called to report to military headquarters, to be taken into the service?

My hon. friend has me at the moment; I did not know they were being called up at that age. I am afraid I have not the informations here just now, but I will have it within twenty minutes and will tell my hon. friend.

If the Minister of
National War Services had been in when the house opened I would have asked him the question on the orders of the day.
The case my hon. friend refers to was a call for military service?
Yes, for army service.

I should like to bring two matters to the attention of the minister. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has drawn attention to the calling up of eighteen year old boys. Could the minister tell us just what the policy of the government is with regard to the calling of conscientious objectors. I know these people are not very popular in the country and one does not court popularity by speaking in their behalf, but it appears that the government is intent upon calling every conscientious objector of military age, regardless of his occupation or of how essential he may be in agriculture or some other industry.
I was surprised yesterday when the minister informed us that men have been detailed from the army back to agriculture and other industries, while at the same time these conscien-
tious objectors, who because of their religious scruples simply will not fight, are constantly being taken out of agriculture and industry, where they are doing a good job of production; and when they refuse to go to labour camps they are even sent to gaol, where they produce nothing but are an expense and liability to the country.
And their wives and children are the sufferers.

That is correct. I have two instances that came to my attention last week, both of which I have brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour, under whom the selective service operates. Apparently nothing can be done, however, to prevent these people from being sent to gaol.
To prevent what?

Apparently nothing can be done to prevent their being sent to gaol. In the first instance this man tells me he is employed in a shoe factory. His employer asked for his postponement, stating that it would be impossible to replace him and that production would suffer if he were called. Notwithstanding that, the man was instructed to go either into the army or into a labour camp. He refused to do either, and apparently he must go to gaol. The second case is that of a man who farms 150 acres of land, with 23 head of cattle, 35 hogs and 6 horses. I have verified these facts. He also has a tractor, which he uses in work for other farmers as well. His father is sixty years of age, and will be unable to carry on the farm if his son is taken away. Yet' that man was haled into the army and, since he was a conscientious objector, was offered the opportunity of going into a labour camp, which he refused. I am told that his case was adjourned for a week to give him a chance to change his mind, but when he still refused to do so he was sent to gaol.
The point is that these people object to paying for the war under compulsion. One of .these men tells me that if he had consented to pay $2 a week to the Red Cross he could have avoided going to gaol or going into the army. I have his statement here to the effect that he was offered the choice of paying $2 into the Red Cross or going into the army. I should like to know the government's position on that matter. On the surface it looks as though there is a prejudice against these men because of their religion. That religion may seem peculiar to some of us, but there would seem to be that prejudice.

War Appropriation-Army
There is no reflection upon the Red Cross?
No, not in the slightest. It was simply that the officers were trying to offer this man an easy way out.
In what district was it that this man who had 150 acres and 23 cows' was refused postponement?
Airound Brampton.
That would be the Toronto district?

No. I am doubtful if this man would have been called from the farm had he not been a conscientious objector.
I have been given the particulars of many farmers who were granted leave to remain on their farms and who to all intents and purposes were no more needed than this man. The second matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is the one we were discussing when the committee rose last night at eleven o'clock, the matter of dependent mothers.

I should like to appeal to the committee in connection with this discussion. I have pointed out to the committee that we have been over two days on item 1 and I do not think ten per cent of the discussion has related to that item. However. I felt that this was the time to permit lion, members to deal with the special things they had in mind or with general topics in connection with the department. My hon. friend has dealt with conscientious objectors. May I say to him with all respect that that matter does not come under the army at all. It has to do with the Department of Labour and national selective service. The next matter he proposes to take up is dependents' allowances which comes under item 2. I wonder if the committee would be prepared to pass item 1, or else confine the discussion to that item so that we may make at least that much progress. The next item will call for a long discussion since it covers pay and allowances which take in a good deal.
I brought this up because it was under discussion last night, but I am quite prepared to wait.
I am trying to get the procedure in the groove, as it were. Does the hon. member for Yale, who is representing the leader of the opposition, think there should be any more discussion on this item?

I think the difficulty arises from the fact that we have adapted ourselves to a course of action which is not strictly in accordance with the rules. We have chosen to adopt this method of clarifying the situation and permitting a great latitude of discussion, but the fact remains that these items have not been committed to the committee. We are scarcely within the rules as we would be if it were a matter of the estimates.
I believe the Minister of Finance put them on Hansard when he made his speech.

But they have not been committed to the committee in the same way as the items of a money bill would be. We have had to devise our own methods of handling this matter, and I am sure the apposition will be ready to accommodate itself to whatever method of conduct may be adopted with the consent of the committee. Considerable discussion has taken place on item 1, but I think a certain amount of latitude was agreed to. I should imagine that most of the questions hon. members would want to ask would fall within the succeeding items.
May I be permitted to bring a matter to the attention of the minister?
Is it under 1?

I have given consideration to what the minister said about item 1 and perhaps item 2. I am referring to a situation which has developed within the last few days. It has to do with the housing of the wives of soldiers and their dependents. I cannot find any item in the list which would cover this except item 4, which covers construction, and that certainly is not the matter with which I wish to deal. I shall not hold up the committee any longer than possible, but what I have to say is supported by a strong resolution, copies of which I believe have reached the hands of the Minister of Munitions and Supply and will probably work back into the Department of National Defence.
I intend to deal with the matter of housing as it affects the families and dependents of soldiers who have gone overseas, as well as soldiers who have returned and their dependents. Many of these are unable to work and they require housing. I ask the minister or his assistant to take note of one or two things. When the wartime housing scheme was first started the Minister of Munitions and Supply did his best to provide housing for soldiers and their dependents by making available in some centres a small number of
War Appropriation-Army

houses which had been built by Wartime Housing Limited. However, when the pressure of production increased, the minister had some difficulty in meeting the demands made upon him.
I think the situation has changed to some extent, if not in all areas at least in my own constituency. I know of one plant the production of which has been reduced to the minimum. Hundreds of men have been laid off in other plants. As the minister has described it, it is now a case of maintenance rather than production. Soldiers and their dependents in this highly industrialized area have suffered considerably. Now that the pendulum is swinging back, the council of my city has taken the matter definitely in hand. As I say, I wish to bring two points to the minister's attention.
I ask him to be good enough to confer with the Minister of Munitions and Supply in an endeavour to have more latitude given to these dependents, and more particularly to those men who are coming back bruised and battered, both mentally and physically, by the war. In order to make my position clear I intend to refer to a resolution passed on Monday night by the council of my city. I shall not attempt to spread the whole text of this resolution upon the record, but I shall read just enough to give the minister the position. Will he just give me his attention? It was moved and seconded:
Whereas this council is definitely of the opinion that members of the armed forces, who have returned from overseas service or from active service in Canada and who have received their discharge papers, should have the opportunity of securing housing accommodation for themselves and their families, by means of rental of wartime housing dwellings.
I repeat, the peak of production in that area has been reached; the pendulum seems to be swinging back so that it is now more or less of a maintenance proposition. The council in its resolution goes on to point out that the dwellings erected by Wartime Housing Limited were put up originally to take care of an emergency situation and that they are not available for members of the armed forces who have been discharged from military service. The resolution goes on to say:
Now therefore this council hereby resolves that the dominion government be petitioned to amend the present regulations governing Wartime Housing Limited dwellings and to provide that members of the armed forces who have returned from duty overseas, or who have been honourably discharged from military service, should be eligible to secure Wartime Housing dwellings for themselves and their families; and that those whose families have been residing in Wartime Housing Limited dwellings during the period of their absence on military service be permitted to continue their occupation of these dwellings.

There is also a reference to unpaid rent accounts. I have searched the records in vain to find anything covering that point; accordingly, I telegraphed to the corporation for instructions, and I received in reply this telegram:
St. Catharines, Ont.
N. J. M. Lockhart, M.P.
St. Catharines paid to Wartime Housing Limited three accounts for rentals unpaid by occupants amounting to a total of $118.12, and has also paid water rates $8.65 and electric light account $6.29.
Herbert H. Smith,
City Clerk.
I can find nothing in the law or regulations that gives Wartime Housing Limited the right to demand a guarantee from a municipality for the payment of rent for a soldier and his dependents. I think it is an unfair imposition to kick that back on to the municipality, because this housing accommodation is being used in some cases for the protection of the wives and families of soldiers who have gone overseas and returned. I suggest that in this matter the minister ask the cooperation of his colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply to see if something cannot be done to rectify the present situation. In that area there are some 800 houses put up by Wartime Housing and there are many soldier families who have not been able to get decent housing accommodation. Some of them are living in hovels. Surely we can do something for the wives and dependents of soldiers who have returned to that area.

I think the quickest way for me to deal with the matter would be to get the letter which was written by the Minister of Finance to the mayors of Windsor and Hamilton, I think it was, setting out the whole arrangement. I shall then give the particulars to my hon. friend. At the moment I would say that what is done is to call to the attention of the municipalities that the matter of housing is not a federal responsibility but a municipal and community responsibility. Notwithstanding that, Wartime Housing Limited has given to the municipalities the use of a certain number of houses which they may want particularly for soldiers' dependents, to be used until other housing is obtainable, and the municipalities looking after the collecting of the rents. . The soldier and his dependents are receiving pay and allowances for the purpose of paying rent. This is just a temporaiy arrangement which was made at the request of the municipalities in order to assist them in carrying out the usual obligations of municipalities in helping to provide housing for their citizens. In Windsor and Hamilton, particularly, the community associations are

War Appropriation-Army
very active in looking up housing accommodation for soldiers' dependents and in indicating or requesting, if necessary, housing of this kind from Wartime Housing Limited. Wartime Housing Limited has put at the disposal of different municipalities a certain number of houses. I have given this information to my hon. friend in advance. I will give him to-morrow the letter written by the Minister of Finance to the municipalities.
May I add in all fairness to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that there is an acute housing situation in that area, which is probably the most highly industrialized in Ontario.
That is St. Catharines?
Yes, including Merritton.
Hamilton too.

Hamilton is also highly industrialized. There was a time when I felt extremely sympathetic toward the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I know that he simply could not give houses that just were not there, and the demand for munitions at that time was so great that munitions had to come first. But now the peak of production has passed in that area. I was in the national selective service office last Saturday morning and I saw at least seventy-five persons arranging for their transportation out of the city. Hundreds have already gone, and I know of several married couples who are planning on moving out because they see production tapering off.
Moving out of Wartime Housing?

Yes, I know of three or four cases personally. The resolution passed by the city council of St. Catharines does not give specific cases. It deals with the problem generally. I could give the minister specific cases of men who have come back from overseas broken down in health who are now on hospital leave from Christie' Street hospital and who just cannot get accommodation for themselves and their families in the St. Catharines area. There is a number of such cases. I am asking the minister to cooperate with the Minister of Munitions and Supply in relieving the housing shortage in that area for members of the armed forces who have returned from overseas and their dependents. I draw to the attention of the minister the situation of the returned men in that area. The city council has been doing its best to search all over for housing for a returned soldier who is mentally unbalanced on account of his war service. Here is an opportunity for Wartime Housing Limited
to give returned men and their dependents some little preference in its housing accommodation.

Yesterday	the minister
promised to give certain information. He said he would tell us, for example, how many men had been detailed for work in shipbuilding yards and other industries. When he is giving us that information, he could perhaps give us further details of the plans with regard to the men called up under N.R.M.A. Just two days ago the minister said that there were about 70,000 men in Canada who had been called into the army under the N.R.M.A. and that of that number
50.000	could be sent abroad to fight; in other words, there were 50,000 fighting men. That same figure of 50,000 fighting men was given also about a year ago by the minister, on May 14, to be exact. At that time he said that there were 50,000 men called up under the N.R.M.A. who could, if the government chose, be sent abroad to fight. A year has passed; 25,000 more men have been called up under the N.R.M.A., and yet to-day we have only 50,000 men, the minister says, fit to fight. I would ask the minister why it is that with this additional 25,000 called up there has been no increase in the number of those who can be sent abroad to fight. The plans for the coming year are that another
12.000	shall be called up. I should like to know whether it is the intention to have any larger number available for fighting, or whether these 12,000 who are to be called this year are simply to be replacements, so that a year from now we shall find, again, that we have only 50,000 N.R.M.A. men who are in a category such that they can do any fighting.

First, with regard to the matter of the men for the shipyards, no soldiers have been detailed for duty with the shipyards. At the request of the Department of Munitions and Supply, in November, commands and military districts were authorized to grant six months' leave without pay and allowances to sixty soldiers who were qualified electricians and who volunteered for employment with the Burrard Dry Dock Company, Limited, Vancouver, on electrical work in connection with the conversion of certain vessels into aircraft carriers. Is that what my hon. friend is referring to?
Yes. Where did these men come from?

Soldiers granted this leave were issued with a free transportation warrant to Vancouver, British Columbia. This expenditure is recoverable by the Department of
War Appropriation-Army

National Defence from the Department of Munitions and Supply, who in turn will recover it from the Burrard Dry Dock company. Transportation on termination of employment is issued under the same conditions. Sixty soldiers volunteered and were released for this employment, reporting to Austin C. Taylor, Wartime Merchant Shipping, Limited, Vancouver, for interview and placement with Burrard. The report shows that recently fifty-seven of these men are still employed, three having terminated their employment due to ill health or other reasons.
I have not information here as to the districts they come from. My hon. friend will notice that commands and districts were authorized to grant six months' leave. They ' were specially trained electricians, and probably would come from quite a number of districts. I will find out.

Were these men N.R.M.A.
men?
I cannot tell. I will find out.

Will the minister find out
where they were sent from?
Yes.

I understand that some, at
least, were sent from eastern Canada.
My hon. friend understands they were volunteers for the work and were given leave.

Is it possible, then, for a
soldier, if he wishes to go into a shipyard, to get leave and go away from the army for an indefinite time?

This was a special case, a special request from the Department of Munitions and Supply to see if we could find them sixty electricians for special work, and we made an order authorizing the districts and commands to give leave to not more than sixty men in the aggregate for the purpose of taking on this work. And they got sixty men.
Is there any similar provision to allow men to go away on leave to work in other industries, war industries or otherwise?

No. Yesterday I read to my hon. friend all the leaves that I know about: coal mining, railways-no, I think it was, detailed for duties on railways-farming, lumbering. I do not know of any others.
With regard to the N.R.MA. personnel strength, the strength as of March 31, 1943, as given to me, was approximately 65,000 enrolled
