in that time. My hon. friend said 30,000, did he not? Nineteen thousand is what I have here.
What year is that?

I beg pardon-enrolled
during nine months up to December 31, 1943, 19,000; making 84,000.
Of course the minister cannot state the figures for the full year.

No, I cannot tell my hon. friend yet. Then, to general service, 3,000; that is to say, men who enrolled and afterwards enlisted for general service; discharges, desertions, deaths, 8,000; making 11,000; leaving the strength as of 31st December, 1944, 73,000, and on leave under these different leaves, about 5,000; leaving the effective strength
68,000.	It is estimated that about 50,000 of these are of a category suitable for overseas. At that rate, taking in the 12,000 planned for this year, I would not think there would be very much increase in the number eligible for overseas; there might be some by taking in the 12,000. The wastage here was 11,000 for the year; at least, the reductions from N.R.M.A.: 3,000 men enlisted and there were
8,000	desertions, discharges, deaths.

How many were discharges
and how many desertions?
I cannot tell.

Can that information be
obtained?
Certainly.
Then the policy is that the number of real fighting men in Canada called up under the N.R.M.A. will not be increased?

What I said was that our provision this year is intended for maintenance. The strength may be increased; that is, if casualties are not in accordance with calculations; if they are, less; or it may be reduced if there are more casualties or if there are some other wastages that we do not know about. But the policy is-and that is what my hon. friend wants-to provide men on a maintenance basis for the present strength.

There is one other question on which I should like the minister to give further information. It has to do with the retirement of officers; he has mentioned it once or twice already in the course of discussion but not in any detail. I think it is a very, very serious question, and I realize that it is a very difficult question. Apparently a large number of officers who have served, many of them since the beginning of the war,

War Appropriation-Army
and some of them overseas, with distinction, and have done good work, are now either being retired or being kept around the depots, told to report back once a week or just keep in touch, not knowing what is going to happen to them, not knowing whether they will be able to do anything further in the army, not knowing whether they should be getting busy about finding some place to earn their living in civilian life; and I think there should be a clear-cut announcement by the minister with regard to these men. It seems to me a tragedy that men can be brought along over this period of time, given many courses, trained until they are efficient officers, and now find that there is no use for them at the present time.
It is true that Canada has not done a great deal of fighting, and casualties-fortunately- have not been very heavy. Probably it will only be a short time until we are having heavy casualties and shall need some of these men. I think the policy regarding them should be given further consideration by the minister. Sometimes I wonder whether the department has not gone too far in the direction of arbitrarily ruling men out at a certain age. Personally I know of many cases where men have gone into the army at great sacrifice and done a good job and now are just hanging around, not knowing what is going to happen to them, becoming disgruntled, and, I think, being treated unfairly. I know the minister would not do that intentionally, but that is the result. These men feel that they are being treated unfairly. Is there not a place for some of them, at any rate, in the administration of the conquered countries, the countries which have been overrun? I believe that we have a course in which Canadian officers are trained for administration work in the overrun countries. Is there not scope here for some of these men? The situation is very serious, and the minister should give further consideration to it, not just say, "Oh, we are modernizing our army and these men have to get out; we thank them for what they have done, but they had better get busy and return to civilian life." That may have to be the answer, but it just does not seem good enough to me under present conditions, in the state of the war at the present time. If this is to be the policy in training these men there is a great deal of money as well as experience being wasted, and I doubt whether the governmental policy at the present time is a wise one. I should like to have an answer.
Let me give the figures with regard to the break-down of the 8,000: 6,500 were discharged, 1.500 deserted.
That is, 1,500 N.R.MA. deserted in the nine months of the present fiscal year?
Yes.
Are these 1,500 still missing?
They may be missing and other men may be picked up. There has been a more or less even flow in the last three months.
That is a very high percentage of desertions.

There have been 11,000 in the four and a half years of war-a net loss of 11,000. In reference to officers, my hon. friend has spoken on a- subject regarding which he is quite right in assuming that I have a very particular interest. I appreciate all that he has said and I considered all that before the present policy was put into effect. The situation is this. We must be realistic and face the hard fact that there are many officers who, as compared with other officers, are not advantageously employable; that is to say, there are officers who can better do the job and whose services are available. What is being done, therefore, is to have these boards sort out the officers, appraise their qualifications, and endeavour to find the best men for the job. That means that there is a substantial reduction in officers, and will be.
Does the minister mean that there are younger officers?

There are some younger officers too. In the last week I have signed ten retirements for officers from twenty-one to thirty. The term- "not advantageously employable" was used, but it meant that those particular officers simply could not do the job and it was felt that they ought to serve somewhere else.
In most cases it is a matter of age.

It is a matter of age and also a matter of the job being abolished. The majority of cases are those of age. Here is the number, and perhaps this will contradict what I said. In the three months from October to January 26, 1,077 officers have been retired, and of that number 212 were recommended for retirement for reasons of age. Of the others, the 800, many were probably seniors-not senior officers but senior in point of age.
Replaced by younger men?

Yes.
War Appropriation-Army
How many retired at their own request?

I have not that statement at the moment. I do not want to refer to what anyone else is doing, or to give that as an excuse for what we are doing, but I have heard no statement which the Minister of National Defence for Air has made this year which has been received with as much applause as the statement he made with regard to the reduction in the number of officers.
You cannot judge policies by applause in this house.
Nevertheless I thought it rather indicated that the policy was a sound one. Someone said to me, "Does that affect you?" I said, "It affects me to this extent that tihe army started ten months ago"-
Do not pay too much attention to applause.

-and I was told that it was a good example to follow. The same situation exists in the United States. They announced a surplus of 65,000 officers and subsequently, through reorganization, the number has been reduced by about half. That is the situation. It is the same in munitions plants, and with executives who have been helping in the war effort. The time has come when we are on a maintenance rather than on a capital basis and the result is a distinct lowering in the number of jobs available. The system we have may not work perfectly, but I do take some pride in it. These officers have personal interviews, and the officers at the depots are in most cases men to whom it could be said at once, "out". At the same time, however, these boards are doing their level best to be sure that there is no job for these men before they are allowed to go. Men come to me frequently and say, "I want an answer yes or no"; but they do not want no. It is the same with these officers. Each individual case is considered by the board an'd passed on by the adjutant general and by the military secretary, whom I regard as the officer's friend. He goes over the cases himself, and it is only after all that is done that the retirements take place. There is a regular procedure and a notice is sent to the officer. Only this morning I gave instructions to see if we could not make that notice a little more human.
M.r. GREEN: It is not very human now.

It is a mimeographed notice that goes to the officer, and after he has held a post for some time it is not a

particularly welcome document. We want to make it as human as we possibly can. The notice is given and the man has an opportunity of making a complaint or a protest or pointing out where he might be used. That is considered by the board, and they make a recommendation as to whether or not the representation shall be entertained, or whether that particular occupation or post which the man suggests might be made available to him. It is only after all that is done that the discharge is made. I take a view opposite to that of my hon. friend. I think officers ought to be discharged faster than they are.
Ought to be what?

I say there should be more speed in connection with the discharge of officers, and I am afraid that the slowness is due to the fact that the board is working at what is an impossible task, nameljy, that of finding employment for all these men. The point is that these men are much better off going back to civil life now than when the rush comes. This is an opportunity for them to go back, and what is detaining them is the pride which they feel in the fact that they have worn the uniform during the war, have helped to build up the army, and have trained men, and feel, therefore, that there should be some place in the army for them while the war lasts.
There was a man of forty-nine in my office the day before yesterday. He has two boys overseas with good service in this war, and he was overseas himself; yet we sent one of these notices to him. The notice took a somewhat more human and intimate form than is usual, but he made an appeal to the minister, as it is his right to do under section 42. I am sending him a letter, as I am bound to, to tell him that I cannot find employment for him. These are tough cases-this is a particularly tough one because there are many that have not nearly the merit it has. I should like to be able to tell the committee that I will try to reconsider the policy, but I cannot reconsider it if administration is to be carried on. It would mean that we would be loaded up with a lot of officers on the payroll, and they would be at least lulled into the security of thinking there is a job for them, only to find, some day, sooner or later, that they have to be cut off. There will have to be many more retirements yet, as there have been in the United States. As regards age, in the United States they are retiring them if over thirty-eight and putting them on the inactive list. We are retiring them at sixty; that is the automatic retirement. I do not say that

War Appropriation-Army
in the United States they automatically retire those over thirty-eight, but those are the only ones taken into account. They look over the men of thirty-eight and see how many can be retired. We are taking them much lower than that, from between thirty and thirty-five. There are not many of these, though there are some.
That is the policy with regard to officers and it is working. That is the machinery we have set up. * We have not just one board for Canada but four boards.- These boards have gone out and got acquainted with these officers intimately in order to assess their qualifications and at the same time to be in touch with the districts to find out what posts there are into which they may be fitted.
About how many officers are facing retirement? How many will have to be retired?

I cannot tell my hon. friend, for this reason: You take officers in the bulk. We might have what may be regarded, as a reserve-this figure is a rough one-of six thousand or something like that in other words, subalterns, a great many officers who have been recently commissioned. It includes older officers as well. You have to keep a substantial reserve, and I cannot say how many of these would be facing retirement. I am not going to make any guess at the moment. Speaking of officers, I should like to make an announcement to the committee before it is made to the press. This is an announcement which will take up the slack in connection with a number of these junior officers, the men who have just graduated or who are in training centres. We are making an arrangement with the British to lend them a certain number-I am not going to say the number, but it is a substantial number-[DOT]
Mr. GREEN. Junior officers?

Junior officers, yes. Under the plan a large number of junior officers, largely of the infantry corps, the Canadian army, are to be lent on a voluntary basis to the British army for service in the European and Mediterranean theatres of war. The plan will permit many captains and lieutenants trained in infantry for overseas duty and physically fit, who otherwise would be unlikely soon to see service abroad, to gain further valuable experience with the British army. The plan is to go into effect immediately. For security reasons the number of officers permitted to go into action with British units under this agreement cannot be disclosed, but a definite limit will be placed on the number to be accepted. The great strength in reinforcement officers which has gradually been
built up in Canada since the outbreak of war makes it improbable that all officers eligible for overseas service will see early action with the Canadian army overseas. The loan plan offers an opportunity to serve with the British forces in the field. Junior officers of the Canadian army in order to take advantage of this plan must, of course, volunteer for this service; that is to say, officers will be given the option of volunteering to go to the British under this plan. They will be on loan for a minimum period of three months. However, their recall has been provided for as and when it is desirable; that is to say, recall by the Canadian government.
One effect of that scheme will be to create for the Canadian army a pool of experienced and, in many cases, battle-trained platoon and company commanders and'potential junior staff officers. The Canadian officers who volunteer for service with the British army will continue to receive their pay and allowances from the Canadian government and at regular Canadian rates, as in the case of the Royal Canadian Air Force crew serving with the Royal Air Force. They will also continue to wear "Canada" badges on their shoulders while serving with the British army. It is pointed out that by volunteering under this plan, Canadian junior officers do not forego opportunities for normal promotion, but while on loan their promotion will be subject to British recommendation and confirmation by Canadian authorities. During the last war many Canadians served as officers in British units in a number of theatres of active operation. The contacts made between the Canadian officers volunteering for this service and the British army should prove invaluable in cementing the cordial relations and understanding already existing between the Canadian and British armies. The loan plan was termed by a senior British officer-that is, in correspondence with the department-as a great contribution to the united war effort. [DOT]
I am afraid there is not very much more I can give in the way of details of the plan. I have already said that they are volunteers. With regard to the ranks of officers we are lending, they are ready to take one captain for each eight lieutenants. They can be recalled at any time. They are to be kept for a minimum of three months. We are asking the officers to agree not to ask for a return to Canada for at least three months. There will be special cases, of course-
Are they going from England or from Canada?

Practically all from
Canada. Pay, allowances and pensions will be paid by Canada. In reference to discipline,
War Appropriation-Army

we want to be particular about that. All adverse reports will be submitted to Canadian military headquarters in London before action is instituted thereon; that is to say, Canada feels that we should keep our hand on that particular feature of the service, particularly since they are on loan. They are subject, of course, to British military law, but in case of a court martial-and I hope there will not be any-sentence must be confirmed by Canadian authorities. We are planning to have a liaison officer at the war office to do nothing but look after postings of these officers and generally watch their interest and the Canadian interest in connection with this plan. I mentioned promotion. It will be to acting rank on recommendation of the British. Normally these would be confirmed by Canadian military headquarters after six months.
Is this open to officers of all infantry units in the Canadian active army in Canada at the present time?

I do not know. The adjutant general is working on it to-day. I do not know exactly whether he is making it to apply to other than those who are actually at corps training centres or at Brockville taking advanced refresher courses, or in camps. I rather think it might be made pretty generally open unless it is a case where in the exigencies of the service a man cannot be spared. My own feeling would be-I was talking to the adjutant general this morning-to give a chance to all junior officers who can be spared. If a man wants to volunteer let him go and substitute for somebody who does not. I may say also I do not think there is any objection in the way of security to saying this. The understanding is that the service is to be restricted to the European and Mediterranean theatres in order to facilitate return in case we should want to recall them.
This is a plan which -I think bids fair to provide some outlet for the energies of a number of junior officers who at the present time are viewing with some concern the prospects of getting overseas soon, and at the same time it provides them with training.

Would it not be wise to make the same provision for some of our officers to be trained with the Australians in the Pacific area? Sooner or later Canada will be fighting the Japanese. It is vital that there should be trained men in that type of warfare. Why are we not giving our men an opportunity to get that training?

Do not let my hon. friend assume we are not. I am not making any 
statement in regard to that at the moment. There are some arrangements along that line in hand.

Just a minute ago, the
hon. member for Vancouver South, who asked a few questions, mentioned N.R.M.A. soldiers. I have in my hand the Canada Gazette of October 30, which contains the National Resources Mobilization Act, army regulations 1943. It is National Resources Mobilization Act army. By virtue of the mobilization act there are two kinds of regulations, those enforced by the Department of Labour and1 those enforced ;by the Department of National Defence proper. These regulations are something like a schedule to an act, and there is a paragraph which I intend to read to show the importance of the regulations and to Show also that by virtue thereof the Department of National Defence has a priority over all.essential industry. This means, therefore, that national selective service is the bunk. Here is the paragraph which is of the utmost importance; listen to this:
In the event of any inconsistency between the provisions of these regulations and the provisions of any other statute or any orders or regulations made thereunder, the provisions of these regulations shall govern.
This is contained in order in council P.C. 7898, which was passed on October 14, 1943, and it means that the regulations established under the order in council for the Department of National Defence have priority over the regulations, also passed by order in council, administered by the Minister of Labour. This has been drafted in an ingenious way. A volunteer is no longer a volunteer according to these regulations; he is a G.S. soldier, under subparagraph (c) of paragraph 6 of the appendix to the order in council I have just mentioned. One would wonder just what is a G.S. soldier; no one ever heard of him before, but it means "general service." The provision reads:
A "G.S. soldier" is a soldier who has voluntarily enlisted for general service during the continuation of the state of war now existing and for the period of demobilization thereafter and who has been taken on the strength of the Canadian army (active) and appointed to a corps placed on active service under section 64 of the Militia Act.
That is the act by virtue of which we have conscription for overseas, but this is the definition of a volunteer; a volunteer is a GB. soldier. Now, what is a N.R.M.A. soldier? That means nothing. He is a draftee, a conscript or a recruit, who has not volunteered as yet. The regulation reads:

War Appropriation-Army
A "N.R.M.A. soldier" is a soldier who has been enrolled and who is undergoing training or performing service or duty under the N.R.M.A. or regulations passed pursuant thereto.
So that a N.R.M.A. soldier is one who has been called by virtue of the regulations giving authority to the Department of Labour. Then amendments were made to this order, but I have only the French copy of the war orders of December 20, 1943, containing the amendments to the army regulations, which were published in the Canada Gazette. I would ask the minister to be kind enough to complete the amendments made by order in council P.C. 9372 of December 7, 1943. I hope that to-morrow he will be able to give us a summary of the amendments to those regulations, which are of the utmost importance.
What I find wrong in this amendment is that it refers to the Army Act, which is not included in the Revised Statutes of Canada but is published in another book. It seems to me that the proper way to legislate is to pass amendments which are complete in themselves, and for the understanding of which it is not necessary to go through the whole library. This amendment contains the definition of a man who reports to a training centre following receipt of an order under the authority of national selective service, and it includes also the definition of a person. Then there is a reference to paragraph 10 of section 176 of the Army Act, and further on there is another reference to the Army Act. May I suggest that the minister tell the office of the judge advocate general that the sections of other acts referred to should be included in amendments affecting any of these orders in council. We have these war orders and regulations, but they mean nothing if each amendment or each order is not complete in itself. I am a layman; I cannot understand the meaning and purpose of that amendment of December 7, and there may be others. It seems only right that members of parliament should be familiar with the regulations affecting the boys in the army or those who may be called by the registrars, and the effect of the call. At the present time it is impossible to inform anyone; we have to write to the department, disturbing the minister or his parliamentary assistant or the other officials, to secure the information we are entitled to have at hand all the time.
I can give my hon. friend the information. That particular amendment just strikes out two words in section 26, if he and I are looking at the same thing.

If the minister will pardon me, I am referring to order in council P.C.
9372 of December 7, 1943; it is one of the first orders in council contained in the war orders which were published on December 20 last. It takes thirteen and a half lines in French.
I thought my hon. friend was asking me what was the effect of P.C. 9372.
Yes, and I should like to know what is the definition of a person according to the Army Act, as well as the meaning of the two references to the Army Act in that order in council.

I think I can give my hon. friend the effect of order in council P.C. 9372 on what I have marked here as order in council P.C. 7989 and the regulations attached thereto. Is that what my hon. friend is dealing with?

No; what I am asking for is the text of the references to the Army Act which are included in order in council P.C. 9372 and other amendments, if any, to order in council P.C. 7989.
